title: Fundamental bound on Wigner negativity generation from environmental collisions
authors: Isaac Layton, Takahiro Sagawa, Ken Funo
abstract: Beyond quadratic potentials, classical evolution laws are typically thought to arise from quantum theory as an approximate description. Here we show that classical evolution laws can emerge exactly, provided the environment interacts with the system via collisions. We use this to derive an inequality that lower bounds the distribution of environmental momentum kicks by the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the potential. We show that violating this inequality is necessary and sufficient for a non-quadratic potential to generate negativity from the set of positive Wigner functions. A simple consequence of this is a lower bound on the heating rate for a quantum system to evolve effectively classically. We illustrate our results using the theory of a levitated nanoparticle subject to photon recoil and background gas collisions. We derive the strength of external potential needed to generate Wigner negative states in an optical tweezer and propose an experimental test of whether a nanoparticle in an optical lattice is operating in a non-classical regime.
summary: This paper derives a fundamental mathematical bound that dictates when quantum evolution, subjected to environmental collisions, remains classically describable (Wigner positive). By analyzing the violation of this bound, the authors predict the generation of Wigner negativity, providing a testable signature of non-classical behavior in systems like trapped nanoparticles.
main_problem: To establish an exact condition for the emergence of classical evolution laws from quantum theory when environmental interactions occur via collisions, moving beyond standard decoherence models.
main_result: The emergence of classicality is governed by a fundamental bound relating the environmental momentum kick distribution to the Fourier transform of the potential; violating this bound generates Wigner negativity.
method: The analysis uses the Wigner representation to track quantum evolution under Markovian open system dynamics, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions via mathematical bounds.
model_or_system: The system is a single quantum particle in a potential $V(x)$, modeled by a master equation incorporating both Gaussian (diffusive) and Poisson (collisional) noise terms. Applications include levitated nanoparticles in optical tweezers.
key_observables: Wigner Negativity, Heating Rate ($\dot{Q}$), Momentum Kick Distribution ($\gamma(k)$), Squeezing Level ($\sigma_p/\hbar k_0$).
important_parameters: Collision rates ($\gamma_{pr}, \gamma_{bg}$), Potential strength ($V_0$), Characteristic frequencies ($\omega, k_0$).
main_assumptions: Markovian open system dynamics are assumed; the analysis often neglects certain scattering effects or assumes specific forms for the environmental interaction.
figures_summary: Figure 1 numerically simulates Wigner function evolution for a particle in a sinusoidal potential, comparing the case with no collisions to the critical collision rate that maintains Wigner positivity. Figure 2 compares required potential strengths against fundamental and heating bounds.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical bound relating $\gamma(k)$ to $V^\circ(x)$, applies this to derive bounds on the heating rate ($\dot{Q}$), and then calculates these bounds and squeezing levels for specific physical systems like trapped nanoparticles.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, quantitative criterion (the fundamental bound) for when quantum dynamics can be accurately mapped onto classical stochastic processes, which is crucial for interpreting experiments involving environmental coupling.
